INTRODUCTION Estonia is on the provisional list of third countries allowed to export milk and milk-based products to the European Union (Commission Decision 95/340/EC). The mission took place from 28 May to 1 June 2001. The mission team comprised three inspectors from the Food and Veterinary Office (FVO) and one national expert. The mission was undertaken as part of the FVO's planned mission programme, and was the first mission in Estonia specifically on the dairy sector. The inspection team was accompanied during the whole mission by several representatives from the Veterinary and Food Board, the central competent authority (CCA). An opening meeting was held on 28 May 2001 with the CCA. At this meeting, the objectives of, and itinerary for, the mission were confirmed by the inspection team, and additional information required for the satisfactory completion of the mission requested. 2. OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The objective of the mission was to carry out an evaluation of the performance of the official services to guarantee that the health rules for the production and placing on the market of milk and milk-based products intended for export to the EU are at least equivalent to those laid down in Chapter II of Directive 92/46/EEC for Community production. In order to assess the system put in place by the Estonian CA, visits to the different levels of the CA, some of the establishments approved for export to the EU, as well as related official laboratories and dairy farms were performed. In pursuit of this objective, the following sites were visited: COMPETENT AUTHORITY VISITS Comments 1 Competent Central 1 authority Regional 4 milk plant laboratories LABORATORY VISITS 3 Private Public 1 LIVE ANIMAL CONTROL SITES Farms FOOD PROCESSING 4 ESTABLISHMENTS - there are no milk collection centres in Estonia Milk processing premises Collection centre 7 3. LEGAL BASES The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: · Commission Decision 98/140/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in third countries1. · Council Directive 92/46/EEC of 16 June 1992 laying down the health rules for the production and placing on the market of raw milk, heat-treated milk and milk based products2. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Previous related missions to Estonia There were two previous OICVP/FVO missions to Estonia, related to milk and milk products. The first (XXIV/2241/97) was carried out in October 1997. While the animal health situation in relation to milk and milk products was considered satisfactory, the public health inspection of the establishments proposed by the Estonian CCA was unsatisfactory. The second mission (XXIV/1412/98) was carried out from 9 to 12 June 1998 as follow-up to the previous one. During this mission, the performance of the CCA was assessed, and one dairy plant, visited previously in 1997, was inspected, as well as one integrated slaughterhouse, cutting and meat processing plant. The outcome of the visits was satisfactory for the dairy plant but unsatisfactory for the meat plant. The report of this mission is available under its specific reference number on the DG (Health and Consumer Protection) internet site at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html 4.2. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Legislation 5.1.1. General The main legal acts in Estonian legislation, relevant for this mission, are the following: 10 · Food Act of 25 February 19993, as amended · Veterinary Act ( Veterinaarkorralduse seadus) of 16 June 19994 · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No. 28 of 21st October 1999 on Hygiene Requirements for the Production of Milk and Milk Products · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.30 of 21st October 1999 on Hygiene Requirements for Producing Raw Milk in a Dairy Farm · Veterinary and Food Inspectorate Directive No. 35 of 15th November 2000 on requirements for veterinary certificates and certification · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.44 of 24th December 1999 on veterinary requirements for importation of animals and animal products · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.12 of 16th of March 5 ("Statutes of the Veterinary and Food Board") An extensive list of Estonian legal acts, corresponding to EC legal acts relevant for this mission is attached after the table of content. The mission team noted that amongst the large number of recently (1995- 2001) adopted Estonian legal acts related to the objective of the mission, two ­ Raw Milk Hygiene Regulation no 30 of 1999, and Milk and Milk Products Hygiene Regulation, no 28 of 1999 ­ refer officially to the relevant EC legislation (Council Directives 92/46/EEC, 89/362/EEC, 89/384/EEC, 94/71/EEC and 95/165/EEC). 5.1.2. Equivalence of Estonian legislation An initial assessment of the Estonian legislation revealed that certain provisions of the Community legislation relevant for the current mission had no equivalent in the Estonian legislation: · no approval required for heat treatment equipment · no formal requirement for official recognition of laboratories carrying out analysis about own-check samples · no official registration of farms supplying milk to EU-premises. 3 RT (= Riigi Teataja, State Gazette) I 1999, 30, 415 4 RT I 1999, 58, 608 5 RTL 2000, 38, 535 11 · no procedure for the withdrawal of farms supplying milk not fulfilling EC requirements In addition, there were no administrative measures in place to ensure that EU exports met these requirements. With regard to quality of raw milk, the current Estonian legislation requires a plate count of 500,000/ml or less, and a somatic cell count of 500,000/ml or less, in raw cow's milk (c.f. chapter 5.4.2). One standard of milk is officially acknowledged. However, in one EC approved plant, the mission team was told by the management that the old system based on the Soviet GOST is still used "internally"- for domestic production. This system comprises three standards of milk: superior, first and unclassified (out ­of-standard). 5.2. CA structure and organisation The Central Competent Authority for matters related to the production, collection and processing of milk in Estonia is the Veterinary and Food Board, Veterinaar- ja Toiduamet (formerly Veterinary And Food Inspection Service, the name changed in 2000). The VFB is working under the Ministry of Agriculture and the Chief Veterinary Officer reports to the Minister of Agriculture. 5.2.1. Management structure The structure of the CCA is described in details in the report XXIV/1412/98 and has not changed since that time. It is a pyramidal structure with direct line of command. 5.2.2. Independence All the officials responsible for the performance of inspections and supervision of establishments enjoy an employment status that guarantees their independence from the establishments for which they are responsible. The staff are paid by the Ministry of Agriculture, but the budget is allocated by the Parliament and cannot be changed by the Ministry. No other occupations for the staff are authorised, unless permitted by the Director (CVO for the CCA and the Director of the Regional Veterinary Centre for the provincial staff). 5.2.3. Resources The budget of the VFB is currently 64 000 000 EEK (ca 11 636 363 ). It is 30 % tax-funded, allocated by the Parliament through the Ministry of Agriculture, together with supervision fees from the food industry, import fees and meat inspection fees. The staff of the VFB is 334 in total, 32 of them in the HQ in Tallinn (20 veterinarians and 12 administrative staff including central bookkeeping). This also includes 118 staff of the Border Inspection Service, 15 of them 12 in the HQ in Tallinn. There are currently vacancies within the VFB, but this is not considered as a problem. The CVO finds the staffing situation satisfactory. 5.2.4. Recruitment & training 5.2.4.1.Recruitment Staff are recruited on the basis of public competition, as required by the Law on Public Service of the 25 January 1995. A yearly accreditation (review) is carried out of all staff members by the Director (and of the Director by a governmental commission). The mission team was told that in one case, accreditation was delayed for six months for one regional VFB director. In addition to officials, there are a number of authorised veterinarians, i.e. private practitioners employed by the VFB on a contract basis. They may be contracted by the CCA for the performance of some official tasks, e.g. TB testing, vaccination or monitoring of hygiene on the farms. The contract is for 1 year, but may be extended for up to 5 years, depending upon the budget situation. There are currently 209 authorised veterinarians in Estonia. All veterinary practitioners in Estonia have to be licensed by the Veterinary and Food Board. To obtain a licence, the following is required: a veterinary diploma, a certificate from the regional VFB and evidence of additional training. A licence is valid for 5 years, and a list of licensed veterinarians is kept by the CCA. Currently, there are 852 licensed veterinarians in Estonia. recommendations.text: To the competent authorities of Estonia To provide the Commission services within one month of receipt of the final report with details of the actions taken and planned, and a time-scale for completion of these actions: - To correct the deficiencies in the designated laboratories, in particular those relating to the analytical methods and to ensure that quality assurance measures are in place. In the meantime, the Estonian authorities have to guarantee that the analyses are transferred to other laboratories that have suitable validated methods and provide reliable results. - To correct the other deficiencies referred to in this report (relating to the Estonian Residue monitoring plan, the procedure for follow-up investigations, availability of veterinary drugs and the control of distribution and use of veterinary drugs) and in particular: - to ensure that the Estonian residue control plan is reviewed in the light of the action plan and sent to the European Commission for approval; - to ensure that all substances mentioned in Annex IV of Council Regulation (EEC) 90/2377 are banned for use in food producing animals whose produce is intended for export to the European Community.

To the Commission Services To closely monitor the actions taken by the Estonian competent authorities to address the above recommendations. 10. ADDENDUM A summary of the response of the competent authority to the draft report including action plan and time table for implementation is given below, nevertheless a copy of the full comments from the CA to the report will be published in the SANCO website together with the final report. 19 The Estonian authorities stated that: - The corrections to the residue monitoring plan for 2001 will be finalised by 15.06.2001. - The (sub)groups of substances not covered by plan will be included in residue monitoring plan for 2002. Sampling at farm level for porcine and poultry will be introduced in the plan for 2002. - In correlation with laboratory capabilities, the sampling will be carried out in variable intervals spread over the whole year. - The targeting criteria in accordance with Commission Decision 98/179/EC will be provided by new decree of Veterinary and Food Board enacted from 01.07.2001. - The laboratories involved in the plan have been provided with uniform reporting formulas to Veterinary and Food Board. - Steps are undertaken in order to remedy the deficiencies in the designated laboratories, in particular those relating to the analytical methods and quality assurance measures. - The contract with the Laboratory of Food Hygiene of Estonian Agricultural University has been terminated from 29.03.2001. Analyses would be carried out in other laboratories within Estonia and in Member States` laboratories (Finland and Sweden). - Estonian State Agency of Medicines will revoke by 1 July 2001 the marketing authorisation of veterinary drugs containing substances listed in Annex IV of Council Regulation (EEC) 90/2377 if those drugs are authorised for use in food producing animals. - A new Medical Products Act is being drafted. Issues as control of distribution of veterinary drugs, import and export control and the establishment of a MRL prior to receiving marketing authorisation of veterinary drugs for food producing animals will be discussed in a working group. 20

The rating goes from very high risk operators (to be inspected four times per year) to very low risk operators (to be inspected only "as necessary"). In this context, VFB distinguishes between traders operating only in the domestic market (classified as very low risk) and traders operating in the EU market (re-classified as low risk). Carriers have been re- classified as low risk and have to be inspected once every three years. VFB and CVC officials stated that those traders classified as very low risk (i.e. to be inspected "as necessary") would only be inspected if a fraudulent activity is suspected or a complaint is received (see paragraph 14). This is not in line with Article 45(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

Adequate arrangements are in place to enable the organisation and planning of regular official controls to monitor and verify that most operators comply with the requirements related to the traceability of ABP/DP throughout the chain. However, the fact that those traders operating only in the domestic market are not subject to regular official controls, limits the ability of the competent authority to ensure that ABP/DP handled by them are channelled and used correctly.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the arrival of consignments of ABP/DP in Estonia is notified via TRACES to the Member States of origin and that this is done on the basis of evidence of arrival at the intended destination, as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: Officials from two CVC visited, declared that the notification of arrival of consignments of products referred to in Article 48(3) consisted only in opening the TRACES document received on-line to check that the the data it contained were correct (e.g. name, address and approval/registration number of the plant of destination). However, physical checks in the plant of destination only took place when the plant was subject to general inspection in accordance with the ABP/DP control plan. The audit team noted that, although the control part in TRACES had been completed for most of the consignments, the time elapsed between the arrival of consignments and the completion of the control part varied from a few days to almost two years. In addition, sometimes, several consignments arriving within several months were controlled in TRACES the same day. These arrangements are not in line with Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 5.2.2 Operators' obligations regarding identification, transport and traceability

Official controls largely ensure that a) operators comply with the relevant rules, and b) officials are able to follow the flow of ABP/DP through the chain if necessary. In addition, the audit team noted good practices by certain officials, who undertook initiatives to better take into account the risk of diversion or misuse of ABP/DP. Nevertheless, the otherwise robust system ensuring that ABP/DP are only used or disposed of in permitted ways is weakened by i) the fact that the said initiatives cannot be considered an integral part of the system for official controls, and ii) gaps in verifying the arrival of consignments of ABP/DP traded in from other Member States.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls on food business operators, producing foodstuffs for delivery to the ultimate consumer, include within their scope the relevant labelling requirements for such products laid down in Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, in particular the verification that the content of the label matches with the data of production as well as the content of the recipes.

citations.text: The deficiencies detected by the CAs in relation to compliance with the requirements set out in Article 3 of Regulation (EU) No 931/2011 were confirmed. In addition in the 5 documentation provided for one establishment, discrepancies were found between the quantities of meat in the recipe and the content of the label. Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain

Three of the establishments visited had effective traceability systems in place: In one, the traceability system covered all processing steps and the FBO was able to demonstrate, through different exercises carried out by the audit team that this system was reliable. Two distribution centres/warehouses visited had robust traceability systems in place, allowing them to follow in real time the goods entering and exiting their warehouses. Both companies had in place a system for detecting anomalies in the matching of incoming and exiting quantities of goods. The audit team noted that the CA in charge of the establishments did not carry out physical checks in the storage/distribution areas when evaluating the traceability system of the companies. The CA stated that due to the working hours of the distribution centres, these on the spot checks could 6 not be carried out. When visiting the storage/distribution areas the audit team was able, using goods physically present, to test of the traceability systems of the companies, with satisfactory results. In another establishment, the traceability system in place was partially effective. All data were recorded manually in different sheets/registers. In principle, this system contained all appropriate information to enable tracking of the identity and quantity of all goods produced, received, processed or dispatched from the establishment. In relation to meat produced in the establishment, the FBO was able to demonstrate that the system functioned as intended. However, in relation to meat sourced from another Member State, used for the production of sliced beef hams, some deficiencies were identified: no document had been issued by the cold store as required by Regulation (EU) No 931/2011; the production batch number was not registered at the heat treatment stage and in storage; and, in addition, the quantities of finished product could not be correlated with production data.

In five of the establishments visited, discrepancies in the quantities of meat used in production were identified by the audit team: In one establishment visited, the traceability relating to a product containing minced meat produced from beef and pig meat (data for four different production days were examined). The documentation presented by the FBO could not demonstrate that the quantity of beef meat used was sufficient for the production of the final product (the discrepancy ranged from 2% to 10 %). The product was labelled as containing beef 50%, pig meat 50%. However, in all cases, pig meat constituted more than 50%. The CAs (central and local level) stated that they had never checked that the quantities recorded as being used were sufficient for the daily production. The CA carried out a 7 follow inspection in the establishment. During this inspection, the FBO stated that the deficiency identified was due to the systematic use of pig meat for standardising the production and not a mix of pig and beef meat in the proportions mentioned in the recipe. The CA confirmed that the FBO had taken action to eliminate the deficiency identified and that a follow up inspection would be carried out at a later stage to verify the implementation of the corrective action; In a second establishment, producing dried meat and frozen cubes of cut meat for supply to catering companies, the quantities of meat, as specified on the consumer did not correspond to the production data. The recipe indicated that 279g of beef meat should be used to produce 100g of final product. However, the quantities actually used were frequently less than specified in the recipe (for example 239g. and 262g.) and occasionally more (for example 303g.). The FBO attributed these discrepancies to differences in the quality of meat bought for the process, stating that the specification of 279 gr of meat yielding 100gr of products had been calculated based on real tests regularly carried out. When reviewing the labelling the audit team was informed by the official responsible of the establishment that this non correspondence between the data contained in the recipe and the data on the label had been identified and that follow up action had already been initiated; In a third establishment visited, producing paprika sausages, the representative of the company responsible for traceability controls, had difficulties in describing the system and its documentation. At the end of the evaluation, the conclusion was that production losses "(animal by-product category 3 material) amounted to 16,5%, exceeding the documented FBO's specifications that these losses should not exceed 5 %; In relation to a composite product for which, based on the recipe, the quantity of ingredients used should have resulted in the production of 750 consumers portions, the number of potions produced was 831. As a consequence, the quantities of ingredients mentioned on the label were not accurate. In particular the quantity of meat present in the composite product was less than 10% although the label stated a meat content of 14%. The composition of two other composite products was checked: for one there was a slight discrepancy between the stated (11 %) and the actual (10.7 %) meat content; for the other, the labelled meat content was correct.

FBOs have implemented the "one step back ­ one step forward" principle of traceability. However, official controls have not been fully effective in detecting some significant deficiencies in the traceability systems in place (see paragraphs 31 ­ 32 below).
The significant deficiencies in the controls (both by FBOs and the CAs) over quantities of meat and ingredients have resulted in inaccurate and misleading labelling of products supplied to consumers

citations.text: The CCA devised and implemented a system for official controls which is risk based and in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Official controls are carried out as required and results are properly documented. A well-organised system for training of official control staff is in place. Nevertheless taking into account all deficiencies identified (see later sections), its effectiveness could be improved. 5.2.2. Implementation of official controls

The CA provided information in a professional, uniform and structured way concerning the tracing to the establishments involved for all 12 randomly chosen samples. This information covered : tracing (one step back ­ one step forward); quantities of meat and products thereof and other ingredients used; labelling; use of additives. The CCA concluded that all samples were traceable and compliant with the labelling and use of additives. Only minor deficiencies in the implementation of Regulation (EU) No 931/2011 have been detected. The audit team analysed the documentation relating to these 12 cases and concluded that, for one case, the documentation did not cover all steps in the process. For the remaining eleven files, the documentation provided was complete in relation to tracing (one step back ­ one step forward) of meat and products thereof and other ingredients used, and in relation to labelling and use of food additives.

The deficiencies detected by the CAs in relation to compliance with the requirements set out in Article 3 of Regulation (EU) No 931/2011 were confirmed. In addition in the 5 documentation provided for one establishment, discrepancies were found between the quantities of meat in the recipe and the content of the label. Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain

Three of the establishments visited had effective traceability systems in place: In one, the traceability system covered all processing steps and the FBO was able to demonstrate, through different exercises carried out by the audit team that this system was reliable. Two distribution centres/warehouses visited had robust traceability systems in place, allowing them to follow in real time the goods entering and exiting their warehouses. Both companies had in place a system for detecting anomalies in the matching of incoming and exiting quantities of goods. The audit team noted that the CA in charge of the establishments did not carry out physical checks in the storage/distribution areas when evaluating the traceability system of the companies. The CA stated that due to the working hours of the distribution centres, these on the spot checks could 6 not be carried out. When visiting the storage/distribution areas the audit team was able, using goods physically present, to test of the traceability systems of the companies, with satisfactory results. In another establishment, the traceability system in place was partially effective. All data were recorded manually in different sheets/registers. In principle, this system contained all appropriate information to enable tracking of the identity and quantity of all goods produced, received, processed or dispatched from the establishment. In relation to meat produced in the establishment, the FBO was able to demonstrate that the system functioned as intended. However, in relation to meat sourced from another Member State, used for the production of sliced beef hams, some deficiencies were identified: no document had been issued by the cold store as required by Regulation (EU) No 931/2011; the production batch number was not registered at the heat treatment stage and in storage; and, in addition, the quantities of finished product could not be correlated with production data.

In five of the establishments visited, discrepancies in the quantities of meat used in production were identified by the audit team: In one establishment visited, the traceability relating to a product containing minced meat produced from beef and pig meat (data for four different production days were examined). The documentation presented by the FBO could not demonstrate that the quantity of beef meat used was sufficient for the production of the final product (the discrepancy ranged from 2% to 10 %). The product was labelled as containing beef 50%, pig meat 50%. However, in all cases, pig meat constituted more than 50%. The CAs (central and local level) stated that they had never checked that the quantities recorded as being used were sufficient for the daily production. The CA carried out a 7 follow inspection in the establishment. During this inspection, the FBO stated that the deficiency identified was due to the systematic use of pig meat for standardising the production and not a mix of pig and beef meat in the proportions mentioned in the recipe. The CA confirmed that the FBO had taken action to eliminate the deficiency identified and that a follow up inspection would be carried out at a later stage to verify the implementation of the corrective action; In a second establishment, producing dried meat and frozen cubes of cut meat for supply to catering companies, the quantities of meat, as specified on the consumer did not correspond to the production data. The recipe indicated that 279g of beef meat should be used to produce 100g of final product. However, the quantities actually used were frequently less than specified in the recipe (for example 239g. and 262g.) and occasionally more (for example 303g.). The FBO attributed these discrepancies to differences in the quality of meat bought for the process, stating that the specification of 279 gr of meat yielding 100gr of products had been calculated based on real tests regularly carried out. When reviewing the labelling the audit team was informed by the official responsible of the establishment that this non correspondence between the data contained in the recipe and the data on the label had been identified and that follow up action had already been initiated; In a third establishment visited, producing paprika sausages, the representative of the company responsible for traceability controls, had difficulties in describing the system and its documentation. At the end of the evaluation, the conclusion was that production losses "(animal by-product category 3 material) amounted to 16,5%, exceeding the documented FBO's specifications that these losses should not exceed 5 %; In relation to a composite product for which, based on the recipe, the quantity of ingredients used should have resulted in the production of 750 consumers portions, the number of potions produced was 831. As a consequence, the quantities of ingredients mentioned on the label were not accurate. In particular the quantity of meat present in the composite product was less than 10% although the label stated a meat content of 14%. The composition of two other composite products was checked: for one there was a slight discrepancy between the stated (11 %) and the actual (10.7 %) meat content; for the other, the labelled meat content was correct.
The significant deficiencies in the controls (both by FBOs and the CAs) over quantities of meat and ingredients have resulted in inaccurate and misleading labelling of products supplied to consumers

citations.text: All holdings in Part II or III that send pigs to either an abattoir or to another holding have to obtain a certificate for the movement, usually issued by an authorised veterinarian, i.e. a "9T" in the case of animals moving from a holding to an abattoir or a "7E" in the case of animals moving between holdings. Both certificates are used to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of various Articles in Decision 2014/709/EU, e.g. articles 3 or 4. These certificates provide information on the ASF testing history (either on a holding or consignment basis) and confirmation of the clinical health of the animals in the consignment. However, there is no certification of compliance with other relevant rules such as 30 day residency of animals, no introduction of new animals on to the holding within 30 days prior to certification or respect of biosecurity rules.

The pre-movement certification of all live pigs provides, in principle, guarantees of compliance with movement rules and thus reduces the risk of disease spread between holdings. However, as authorised veterinarians do not perform pre-certification checks correctly (i.e. sampling procedures and verification of residency periods) and the verification system does not pick-up failures in the system, the measure is not very effective, which hinders this reduction of risk.

All live pigs arriving at an abattoir are accompanied with a "9T" health certificate as described in finding 29. The official vet in an abattoir relies on the "9T" and the list of holdings which comply with Article 3, 3a or 4 of Decision 2014/709/EU in order to assess whether pigs are eligible for the derogations under this Decision. If deemed eligible, a triangular national health mark is used for fresh pig meat, pig meat preparations and pig meat products from III which allows circulation on the national market. Eligible pigs from Part II receive the oval health mark and can circulate on the EU market.
For pig meat, the reliability of this system is undermined by the insufficient assurance that pigs comply with residency and standstill requirements. 17

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take measures to ensure that official controls on dairy farms are consistently carried out in compliance with the requirements of Articles 9 and 54 of Council Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based upon conclusion 24. , first bullet point.

citations.text: Both farms visited by the audit team had been inspected recently without any non- compliances being reported. One farm had less than 50 cattle in total (dairy cows, calves and heifers), kept tethered when indoors but grazing at pasture at the time of the visit, and produced milk exclusively for direct sale. The other had over 1000 dairy cows kept in loose housing conditions: In the smaller farm the cattle stalls were too short for the length of the animals present but, although both the AV and the County veterinarian agreed with this assessment, neither the County veterinarian nor the AV had reported it as a non- compliance nor required in writing any actions to rectify the problems (which is not in line with the requirements of Article 9 and 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004). This was because the farmer was aware of the issue and had a refurbishing project that was supposed to address it for at least some of the animals but nevertheless had not yet done so at the time of this visit. Bedding was present in the stalls and the audit team noted that the animals did not show significant lesions on their hind legs that would indicate inadequate welfare due to the shortness of the stalls. 10 In the larger farm the housing facilities were in line with requirements, and the cattle showed no signs of inadequate welfare other than some indications of mild lameness. Farm management informed the audit team that lameness was indeed an issue as there was a relatively high incidence of digital dermatitis which they had been addressing (and managing to decrease the trend) but had until now been unable to fully control.

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that the system for regular official controls on the welfare of dairy cows includes also verification of the requirements of the Council of Europe recommendation concerning cattle that support the requirements of Directive 98/58/EC. Recommendation based upon conclusion 24. 14

citations.text: Official controls on animal welfare of dairy cattle are performed on a regular basis, based on risk-assessment (see also paragraphs 16 and 17): by County veterinarians on the welfare of calves, in the case of farms with more than six calves; by AVs for all other types of cattle, so all of both dairy and beef cattle of all ages. 8 Or ad-hoc, by County veterinarians: to follow up on reported non-compliances by the AVs who are not empowered to impose sanctions. Due to that, if sanctions are envisaged, any non-compliance with animal welfare requirements reported by an AV must be confirmed by a County veterinarian; or as a consequence of complaints.

County veterinarians informed the audit team that the ad-hoc control focuses in principle on confirming the presence of the reported non-compliance, or the cause of the complaint. A full animal welfare control (which would use the instruction and checklists for County veterinarians that has the complete requirements for cattle instead of only those from Directives 98/58/EC and 2008/119/EC) may be done during these ad-hoc visits but usually only if additional non-compliances are noticed during the visit.

The number of animal welfare non-compliances in dairy farms reported by the AVs and County veterinarians is low: out of 2006 controls in 2013 and 1487 controls in 2013 in cattle farms (dairy and beef cattle) there were respectively 51 (2.5%) and 30 (2%) animal welfare non-compliances reported. Additionally, in the two Counties visited there were almost no complaints related to animal welfare issues in dairy farms within the last three years. Since the regular controls of dairy cattle other than calves are carried out by the AVs and their instructions and checklists do not include the complete cattle requirements (see also paragraph 13), there is no regular verification of compliance with 9 those complete requirements in dairy cattle, other than calves, except in exceptional circumstances.

recommendations.text: To ensure that establishments are approved only where they meet the relevant requirements and that approval conditions are maintained in order to comply with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: This establishment was fully approved by the CA on 11 September 2015 as fulfilling all the structural and operational requirements. However, on 14 March 2016, the CA carried out a comprehensive inspection and a list of 15 shortcomings was noted. This list contained among others shortcomings related to Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP), labelling, traceability, cold chain, food contact materials, water quality and other prerequisites.

The audit team visited three small establishments and noted they did not meet all the relevant EU requirements. Two establishments in particular had significant shortcomings related to structure and lay-out (see chapter 5.2.1) Conclusion on registration / approval of FBOs

There is a system in place for approval and registration of establishments. However, the implementation of the approval procedure is not satisfactory as it does not ensure that approved establishments fulfil all the relevant EU requirements.. 5.1.4 Prioritisation of official controls Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 4 Findings
Nevertheless several shortcomings identified by the audit team, mostly related to approval and pasteurisation procedures/process had not previously been identified by the CAs.

In two of the four counties visited, the official reports did not reflect the non- compliances identified by the audit team in the four establishments visited. The officials in charge of the establishments concerned completed the control checklists without identifying any relevant shortcomings present in the establishments. Also the approval of three establishments visited in these counties had not been carried out correctly (establishments approved without fulfilling all the relevant requirements, see paragraphs 19 and 20)

The audit team noted in particular:- - In two milk processing establishments, none of the lay-out and structural shortcomings had been identified by the CA. Lay-out and structure did not prevent crossing of flows of operations and possible cross-contamination of raw/pasteurised and packed/unpacked products. In one of these establishments, the critical control point for pasteurisation was not properly identified and not properly monitored. In the other establishment, evidence could not be provided to the audit team that the time-temperature combination (67o-69o for 10 minutes) applied by the FBO had an equivalent effect to those indicated in EU legislation for achieving pasteurisation. The CA stated that this equivalency was verified by the FBO by performing an alkaline phosphatase test, however the FBO failed to produce any results of this test. In addition, the audit team noted that the heat treatment process was not continuously monitored by the FBO. - In another establishment the critical control point for pasteurisation had been properly identified but the recorded monitoring procedure was different from the real one. The pasteurisation temperature was much lower than the one described in the HACCP plan. However, this situation did not pose a risk to public health as the initial temperature was sufficiently high. - In another establishment, a similar situation occurred. However, in this instance the audit team noted that the temperature applied by the FBO fell below legal requirements. Evidence that such heated though unpasteurised milk had not been 10 used in the production of dairy products could not be provided to the audit team. The audit team was informed that this situation was caused by a failure of the automatic equipment, and/or the recording system, which had not been noted or assessed by the FBO and not recorded by the CA. - In another establishment the FBO could not provide evidence that the time ­ temperature combination used for pasteurisation met legal requirements. - The size of premises in one establishment, and in particular the number /size of the maturation rooms, were inadequate in relation to the volume of products processed.

In one establishment visited, the flow and space available for crates used for finished products was not satisfactory. Dirty crates were used for packing of products. The CA had identified the problem with storage, but had not drawn any conclusions or made written recommendations for the correction of the problem.
In one establishment, with limited space and with intermediate products exposed to cross-contamination, black mould was noted on wooden support structures in the maturation room.

In two establishments visited, the water sampling plan had, according to the local CA, been approved and is controlled by the Health Board. The FBO had implemented the water sampling in accordance with their plans. However, in both cases the monitoring for chemicals, under this sampling plan, did not cover all the parameters foreseen in Directive 98/83/EC, and in particular acrylamide, vinyl chloride, and bromate. The CA referred to an explanation provided by the Health Board, according to which analyses of these parameters was found to be unnecessary in dairy establishments and as such, these were not required.

In one case, based on the establishment's water consumption, organoleptic and microbiological parameters (check monitoring) should have been checked quarterly and all parameters in Article 5 of Directive 98/83/EC (audit monitoring) annually. Instead, the check monitoring had been carried out by the FBO once a year and the audit monitoring every ten years. The CA and the FBO were unable to explain the reason for this reduced frequency. Conclusion on general and specific hygiene requirements

Official controls for verification of FBOs compliance with the general and specific hygiene requirements are in place. However, the controls are not effective as they are not able to identify significant problems at establishment level. As a consequence the system in place does not satisfactorily verify that the establishments comply with the relevant EU requirements. 5.2.2 Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points based systems Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Articles 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. 11 Findings

recommendations.text: To verify that Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points based systems in the milk processing establishments are designed and implemented in accordance with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004; in particular that all critical control points are properly identified and monitored.

citations.text: However, in five plans reviewed by the audit team significant risks and corresponding critical control points had not been identified by the FBO and this situation was not noted by the CA (see paragraph 63).

In several cases, the FBO did not follow the procedures as described in the HACCP programme. In particular, for pasteurisation procedures, where a certain amount of unpasteurised milk could go for products supposed to be made exclusively from pasteurised milk. This was not identified by the CA.

In one establishment records on the pasteurisation and the cleaning programme were kept both on paper and on computer. However, the times recorded did not reflect in all cases the action being carried out. Thus, for example, the time of pasteurisation as recorded on paper could be logged as cleaning time in the computer. Based on these records it was impossible to determine if the current activity at any given time was pasteurisation or cleaning. This brings confusion concerning the amount of milk really pasteurised. Conclusion on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points based system

citations.text: MoRA is also responsible for the allocation of sufficient budget for controls and for the supervision of the control and certification tasks conferred to EAB and VFB. Supervision must take place once every five years in accordance with national rules. It is carried out either by MoRA´s internal audit team or by outsourcing it to external companies. For example, the audit team reviewed a report of an additional inspection carried out at an operator who runs conventional and organic units as described in paragraph 35 above. recommendations.text: To ensure that an adequate number of additional and unannounced visits are carried out in accordance with the risk profile of operators, as required by Article 92c(2)(b), (c) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Recommendation based upon conclusion No 43 23

citations.text: The audit team noted that the manner in which inspections are announced to operators differ between EAB and VFB. VFB generally carries out all inspections unannounced while EAB allows for short prior warning of up to 48 hours being given to farmers, even for additional inspections that according to Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 should be primarily unannounced. Although the audit team fully understood the reasons given by EAB that in some cases it is difficult to carry out an inspection at farmers without prior warning, this should be the exception (for duly justified cases) rather than the rule. 9 As a consequence of this shortcoming, Estonia is not in the position to fulfil the requirement of Article 92c(2)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 that at least 10% of total inspections and visits are carried out unannounced, and that these are planned according to the level or risk.

Additional inspections are planned at the beginning of the year by EAB and VFB. The audit team noted that both CtrlAs generally achieve the number of inspections planned. However, the manner in which EAB and VFB select operators for additional inspections differ greatly. VFB follows the working document agreed by Member States and issued by the European Commission, which instructs how to classify operators in risk categories following risk assessment made of them all. VFB thus uses a number of criteria (e.g quantities produced or traded, past non-conformities, potential of exchange of products, e-commerce, sales or pre-packed or unpacked products, subcontracted operations).

Every operator is rated for each criterion and given a final score based on the aggregated scores. The operators are selected for additional inspections in descending order starting with the one with the highest score. There are also additional factors that can be taken into account but not rated with points (e.g. textual remarks from the inspector, operator under control of EAB and VFB).

EAB sets up the risk criteria annually, with some criteria being used each year (e.g. past irregularities, risk of mixing organic and non-organic products) while others are introduced based on a thematic approach for the year in question (e.g. small potato growers with land area between 10-50 hectares for which complaints were received). EAB 10 then groups the operators under each of the criteria. Operators may be selected for additional controls based on one criterion only, also taking into account input from inspectors. This not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, as no individual assessment is made to determine the risk profile defined for each operator, taking into account all the criteria established by EAB, or at least the three compulsory criteria required by the said article.

Even if selecting the operators based on one criterion only can be useful to detect non- compliant operators, the inspections carried out on this basis should not be counted as part of the minimum, required by Article 92c(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, of 10% of operators that must be subject to additional inspections based on their risk profile.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the manner in which inspections are announced to operators differ between EAB and VFB. VFB generally carries out all inspections unannounced while EAB allows for short prior warning of up to 48 hours being given to farmers, even for additional inspections that according to Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 should be primarily unannounced. Although the audit team fully understood the reasons given by EAB that in some cases it is difficult to carry out an inspection at farmers without prior warning, this should be the exception (for duly justified cases) rather than the rule. 9 As a consequence of this shortcoming, Estonia is not in the position to fulfil the requirement of Article 92c(2)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 that at least 10% of total inspections and visits are carried out unannounced, and that these are planned according to the level or risk.

The audit team noted that according to the Organic Farming Act, samples may be taken in the framework of horizontal controls and not necessarily with the purpose of verifying compliance of operators with the requirements of the organic regulation. For example, VFB elaborates its sampling plan in the framework of food safety controls, which generally include testing for the detection of multi-residues of plant protection products.

When the products sampled happen to be organic, the samples are counted for the 5% target required by article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The products selected for sampling are categorised according to pre-defined criteria (products most commonly purchased by Estonian consumers, results of samples from the previous years, OFIS (Organic Farming Information System) notifications and internal detections, risk of use 14 of substances extensively used in conventional production, products not tested before) and covering all stages of the food chain). However, VFB does not use the risk assessment described in paragraphs 36 and 37 to select the operators, which is not in line with the said article.

Moreover, VFB also counts the samples of products of animal origin, taken by VFB at primary producers in the framework of food safety controls, towards the 5%. This is not correct as the legal requirement refers to the taking of samples at operators under organic controls (and according to risk assessment under organic legislation) and not under food safety controls. VFB does not know the risk profile of primary producers as they are not under its control and this information is not shared by EAB.

EAB selects the operators based on the risk assessment implemented for deciding on additional inspections. However, as described in paragraph 38, the assessment is not fit for purpose and does not serve to identify the operators who pose the highest risk.

Moreover, EAB takes samples from final products intended for consumption and rarely from soil or non-edible plant parts. This and the fact that many samples are taken during storage of harvested products (e.g. 40% in 2020) reduces the likelihood of detecting substances not authorised in organic production. This is because the presence of residues of plant protection products decreases from the moment of application, and even faster from fruits than from plant parts or soil. Furthermore, if the sample is positive, it may be more difficult to determine from a sample taken from storage whether the cause was spray drift from neighbouring fields or use on the field itself, since it normally cannot be determined from where in the field the sampled material came. As described in paragraph 34, EAB does not take samples from products of animal origin at primary producers.

The fact that samples are not taken at the most risky operators or at the most suitable time and place can explain the low number of samples that have tested positive for the presence of unauthorised products in the 2020 and 2019 campaigns. As an example, there were only four positive results in 2020 out of 147 samples taken. Of these, two were taken on suspicion by the EAB inspector and one taken by VFB at catering facilities not in the control system).

Moreover, the procedures for the taking of samples mentioned in paragraph 53 do not contain detailed guidance on how to collect samples from the fields or to evaluate the results of the samples taken. Both CtrlAs stated that any presence of unauthorised substances is considered as a potential irregularity and an investigation is launched in all cases. As an example of this, the audit team was shown a case where an operator raised a complaint to EAB against a wheat producer following the analytical results of a sample taken during the operator's own checks. EAB launched an investigation including a visit to the wheat producer, who attributed the presence of the residue to spray drift from a non- organic neighbouring plot. EAB asked the plant protection and fertilisation department (responsible for horizontal controls at the non-organic farmer) to follow-up and confirm whether the thesis of spray drift was plausible or not. Based on the reply of the plant 15 protection and fertilisation department, EAB concluded that the spray drift was not plausible (see also paragraph 84).

The case above shows good internal co-operation within EAB and enabled it to take a correct ad-hoc decision. However, it alone cannot ensure that an appropriate decision is made in all cases without a specific sampling methodology allowing for the assessment of the laboratory results to conclude that the presence of the unauthorised substance was the result of its use or spray drift. Conclusions on sampling and laboratory analysis

recommendations.text: To have arrangements in place to ensure consistency of official controls to verify measures taken by primary operators prior to and during harvest to control microbiological contamination arising from the air, soil, water and fertilisers in line with the provisions of Article 5(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the checklist for primary producers covers both sprout- producing establishments and other primary producers of FNAO. The audit team noted that this checklist has included the general questions from Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 for primary production (questions 5(a) to (g) of part A.II on hygiene provisions). However, these general questions have not been deployed into more specific control points and inspectors lack of criteria regarding the suitability of measures to be implemented by operators to address microbiological risks.

The inspectors interviewed during the audit were aware of the guidance document on addressing microbiological risks in fresh fruits and vegetables at primary production through good hygiene (2017/C 163/01 (2)). However, the CA has not availed of the opportunity to deploy this guidance document into the inspection procedure. Inspectors have not received formal training regarding this guidance, and no specific guide or instruction has been given to set clear criteria to have a common and consistent understanding on what measures are expected to be found in primary production establishments and how to assess their suitability for reducing microbiological risks. Seeds for sprouting and sprout-producing establishments

The official control system is able to identify and rectify shortcomings of processors of FNAO. However, the lack of sufficiently detailed guidance for the use of existing checklists for controls of primary producers, compromises the consistency of official controls aimed at verifying that operators have taken appropriate measures to minimise microbiological risks, pre-farm gate. This hinders the capacity of the CA to identify and react to non-compliances. 15

The audit team noted that control points within the checklist for primary producers of FNAO are not detailed enough to guide the inspector in the type of measures that are expected to be implemented by primary producers to reduce microbiological risks associated with activities prior to and during harvest. As such, this checklist does not specifically address, among others, the need for "field toilets" and "handwashing facilities" for farms growing crops to be eaten raw and considered of high risk (see paragraphs 54 and 55). As such, and in the absence of specific notes uploaded to the system, it is not possible to corroborate whether such measures have been systematically verified during the official control. The internal audit on FNAO in 2019 also concluded 19 that "it is not clear from the inspection reports what exactly was assessed in terms of primary production and what weaknesses existed in terms of primary production". Conclusion on procedures for performance and reporting of official controls and other official activities

The CA has procedures, instructions and checklists that enable the CAs to perform official controls of FNAO establishments and for establishments seeking approval, in a uniform fashion. However, checklists lack sufficient guidance to address specific measures taken by operators to prevent microbiological risks pre-farm gate. This can compromise the consistent performance of official controls by the inspectors.

recommendations.text: To ensure that actions are taken to determine the origin and that measures taken by the operator remedies the non-compliance and prevents further occurrences in the cases where pathogen Listeria monocytogenes is detected in establishments producing ready to eat foods of non-animal origin, as required by Article 138(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In two of these FBOs, some of the test results showed positive findings for Listeria monocytogenes, and operators were requested to take measures to address this problem. Operators agreed to carry out deep cleaning and sanitation and additional samples were taken with negative results. According to the recorded information on the official control reports, own-check monitoring plans were amended, increasing the number of environmental samples to detect Listeria monocytogenes from once a year to once every quarter. In another case, the frequency set by the FBO was twice a year. These proposed FBOs' own-control plans were accepted by the CA.

However, this is not in line with an expert opinion on surface sampling which is embedded in the Estonian document "Guidance on planning and reporting on sampling and reporting of microbiology and gluten-free labelled food during monitoring in 2021". This Estonian expert opinion indicates that if there is a positive Listeria monocytogenes result, the frequencies for analysis (environmental sample, end-product) should be much higher i.e. once a week. Other Control Systems

The CA has properly included in the official controls the monitoring of environmental samples to detect Listeria monocytogenes. However, its acceptance of monitoring plans from FBO where positive results had been found which proposed only a marginal increase in the frequency of tests (and moreover much lower than frequencies suggested in national guidance), calls into question the appropriateness of its measures to ensure that operator effectively remedies the situation and demonstrates effective preventive measures, as required by Art. 138(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2019/625. recommendations.text: To ensure that samples are dispatched to the laboratories promptly and that the storage and transport conditions, prior to the arrival at the laboratories, are suitable to ensure analyte stability and sample integrity for each analyte/matrix combination.
recommendations.legal_basis: Point 7 of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2021/808.

citations.text: Pending dispatch to the laboratory, samples can be stored in fridges or freezers, depending on the matrix and analyte concerned, under the control of the official sampler. Interviewed officials indicated that samples taken at slaughterhouses were sometimes be placed into the transportation boxes without preceding chilling/freezing.

National instructions do not specify any time limit between sampling and sample dispatch to the laboratory and, at the time of the audit, the time taken between sampling and dispatch was not actively monitoring by the AFB or Regional Specialists. Data requested by the audit team showed that, although most samples arrived at the laboratories on the day of sampling or one to two days afterwards, in some cases the time between sampling was much longer (up to 42 days). The AFB immediately responded to this new information, identified the main source of the delays and put in place corrective action.

The residue monitoring plan is generally implemented in accordance with planned arrangements. However, some identified shortcomings (i.e. inconsistencies regarding announcement of sampling visits to farms, delays sending samples to laboratories, the lack of supervision from the central and regional competent authorities to ensure that sampling in aquaculture takes place at all stages of production and, for other commodities, that repeated sampling of the same producer is avoided), cumulatively have a negative bearing on the effectiveness of official controls on residues.

The audit team checked the acceptance/rejection system for incoming samples by the three national laboratories and saw that this generally addressed control of the accompanying documentation, checks of the seals and general condition of the samples. Temperature of the samples at the time of reception was not controlled in any of the laboratories thus the provisions established by EU legislation (25) to ensure the samples' legal, scientific and technical validity were not fully addressed. During the audit, representatives of two national laboratories stated that temperature control of all incoming samples would commence from 1 October 2021 and that a pertinent quality control document was under preparation.

Notwithstanding the fact that all of the laboratories are duly accredited, operate methods included in their respective scopes of accreditation and that the laboratories' performance in proficiency tests has been generally satisfactory, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods and in the implementation of internal quality control procedures, combined with the absence of designation of sub-contracted laboratories and lack of temperature controls on incoming samples, weaken confidence in the reliability of analytical results and thus the effectiveness of the residue control system.

recommendations.text: To ensure that all analytical methods are comprehensively validated/verified and that method performance parameters are evaluated against the criteria established in EU legal acts and taken into consideration when the conclusions on each method's fitness for the intended use are made.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 3 of, and Chapters 1 and 2 of Annex I to, Regulation (EU) 2021/808.

citations.text: The screening method for aminoglycosides in muscle was initially validated as a confirmatory method in line with pertinent EU requirements (26). However, due to consistently and unacceptably high reproducibility levels, the conclusion stated that the method would be used only as a semi-quantitative screening method. The audit team noted that no further elaboration/evidence was provided in a documented traceable manner to demonstrate that the method had a false compliant rate lower than or equal to 5 % ( error) (27).

The screening method for antibacterial agents in kidney was verified in line with applicable EU provisions (28). However, the documentation submitted for the screening method for antibacterial substances in milk suggested that only 12 samples (per concentration) were used for the verification, which did not correspond to the minimum number of 20 samples required to ensure that the method had a false compliant rate lower than or equal to 5 % ( error) (27).

The documentation submitted regarding the method for hormones in urine and serum demonstrated that the repeatability and reproducibility values were consistently identical which is not in line with EU requirements (29). These phenomena were not commented on or discussed in the validation report and the method was considered fit for purpose as a confirmatory method. The situation with non-commented identical repeatability and reproducibility values was seen for certain fortification levels in several other validation files scrutinised by the audit team, questioning the validity of the laboratory's conclusion that said methods were fit for their intended use.

The audit team noted numerous occasions where recovery or/and reproducibility values exceeded the ranges established in the EU legislation (30), e.g. for diclazuril and salinomycin in the coccidiostats confirmatory method. These occurrences were largely not evaluated/discussed in the validation files and consequently not taken into account for the decisions on methods' fitness for purpose.

The audit team noted that in all of the validation files scrutinised, stability was mentioned as a performance characteristic. However, the procedure for its assessment was substantially different from the protocol suggested in EU law (31) and essentially not adequate to provide sufficient knowledge on the stability of analytes, in particular in matrix. Combined with the absence of a temperature check on the incoming samples (see finding 51), this might influence the test results. recommendations.text: To ensure that in testing laboratories adequate quality control procedures are put in place, consistently implemented during routine screening and confirmatory analysis and assessed against established criteria.
recommendations.legal_basis: Chapter 3 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2021/808.

citations.text: The audit team scrutinised the implementation of internal quality controls for four samples (analysed in 2020-2021 by the largest national laboratory) where measurable quantities of veterinary medicinal products were found. In two of the four samples (diclofenac in bovine muscle and antibacterial substances in raw milk, both from 2020), the audit team observed that no matrix-based `positive control' samples were included in the analytical runs, which is not fully in line with EU requirements (33). The laboratory representative explained that this was due to absence of pertinent control samples and that this practice was discontinued since the beginning of 2021.

The audit team observed the control charts for the methods used for the four samples scrutinised and found that: a. in the control chart for penicillin V, the trueness based on results of more than 30 analytical runs was 184%, which substantially exceeds the range established in EU law (80-120%) (34). While the laboratory representative was aware about that breach, no action had been taken to address the situation. b. for the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs method, very few points were available due to the low number of analytical series (since the relevant samples are collected during a narrow time window to ensure that the laboratory processes those in one go). This precluded the creation of a functional control chart.

For the screening method for antibacterial substances in milk, no sufficient evidence was submitted that quality control samples had been regularly used for the purpose of verifying ongoing method performance, which contradicts pertinent EU requirements (33).

For the same method, the audit team noted that once a suspect non-compliant result was identified, the same sample was run up to three times more before a decision was made to confirm the screened positive result with a chemical confirmatory method. This practice may lead to the situation where non-compliant results would not be identified due to false-compliant outcome of screening testing, is not in line with legal requirements (27), and contradicts the bioassay manual.

Notwithstanding the fact that all of the laboratories are duly accredited, operate methods included in their respective scopes of accreditation and that the laboratories' performance in proficiency tests has been generally satisfactory, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods and in the implementation of internal quality control procedures, combined with the absence of designation of sub-contracted laboratories and lack of temperature controls on incoming samples, weaken confidence in the reliability of analytical results and thus the effectiveness of the residue control system.

According to the CA, staff from central level may get involved in the approval process (on-site verification) if the regional inspectors so demand. 6

The audit team noted that this practice entails the risk that the conditions of approval of fishery products establishments are assessed differently by each inspector responsible. This is because the supervision system, as currently implemented, is not designed to identify and tackle performance weaknesses of individual inspectors (see paragraph 12.b) and, as observed by the audit team during the on-site verification, some inspectors had different understanding and views on certain topics (i.e., hazard analysis, pre- requisite programmes and documentation requirements, traceability) than other inspectors had on the same topics (see paragraph 55).

The audit team noted that certain elements in the establishments visited were assessed differently by the inspectors involved. This resulted, in establishments visited by the audit team, in one establishment having in place a properly designed, implemented, monitored, and documented pest control plan, while another establishment had in place a poorly designed, implemented and documented one. c. Fish fillets were left for long periods without ice with their temperature rising to 11 ; packaged ready-to-eat fishery products (spiced sprat fillets) were left outside the chiller for as long time as it was necessary to pack and assemble an entire pallet with the product. c. recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently check that feed business operators meet the requirements for hazard identification in their respective hazard analysis and critical control point plans, and that the result of this assessment is recorded in the report of said official controls.

citations.text: In all five establishments visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection reports, the operators' HACCP plans and interviewed the inspectors on their assess- ment of these plans. In every inspection report the audit team identified deficiencies in the inspectors' assessment of the hazard identification part of the operators' HACCP plans. Whilst some of the inspectors were able to correctly identify these deficiencies when interviewed, the inspection reports did not refer to these. The audit team saw 5 that the hazard identification part was either incorrect (certain hazards which would be relevant for the product being manufactured were not mentioned e.g., pesticides, my- cotoxins, dioxins and heavy metals) or was insufficiently specific (lacking the level of detail necessary for a proper hazard identification (as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) and the consequent risk assessment. The operators were thus unaware that there were shortcomings in the hazard identification part of their HACCP plans.

The planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and allows for official controls to be carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with and appro- priate frequency. recommendations.text: To ensure that, in the event of established non-compliance(s) being identified, the central competent authority imposes appropriate measures to ensure that the operator concerned remedies the non-compliance and prevents further occurrences.

citations.text: The audit team reviewed documentation for six sampling and inspection-related feed safety and feed quality non-compliances. The feed inspectors could provide evidence (official reports) that follow-up of these non-compliances had been carried out and that, in the context of follow-up, the FeBOs had submitted evidence of the corrective actions they had taken. The audit team noted that in five of the cases the follow-up was not effective ­ i.e., the non-compliance persisted and thus the measures taken by the competent authority to ensure operator remediation and prevent further non- compliances, as required by Article 138(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, were inef- fective. For example, in a case where the label of compound feed was identified by the feed inspectors as incorrect, the FeBO subsequently modified the label, but the label remained inaccurate even after this modification and the new error had not been spot- ted by the feed inspector. In another case, the root cause of the non-compliance was that the FeBO had used a premixture (for the production of compound feed) which contained some feed additives at a lower concentration than declared on the label. The FeBO continued to use this premixture for production of further batches of compound feed without changing either the recipe or the label and thus the non-compliance per- sisted. Conclusion on the actions taken on non-compliances

Notwithstanding the fact that the competent authority took actions when non- compliances had been identified in the course of official controls, the competent au- thority's measures to ensure that the operator remedied the non-compliance and pre- vented further occurrences were ineffective.

recommendations.text: To ensure that all analytical methods used for residues testing are fit for their intended purpose.

citations.text: The auditor reviewed in detail the screening methods for antimicrobials (Group B1a) in milk (commercially available assay) and in kidney. The approach to verify the performance of the methods in the provided reports was generally acceptable, however comparison of the CC for these methods to the maximum residue limit (MRL) set out in EU legislation (13), indicat- ed that neither method met the required level of sensitivity for a number of analytes, which is not in line with pertinent EU requirements (14). Conclusions on laboratories and method validation

Notwithstanding the progress that has been made and that the actions taken to rectify defi- ciencies identified during the 2021 audit concerning method validation are largely sufficient, shortcomings in relation to the sensitivity of the screening methods for antimicrobials and the approach used to evaluate relative matrix effect undermine the effectiveness of the cor- rective actions taken.
