recommendations.text: To ensure that the supervision arrangements in place are adequate and able to ensure the effectiveness, appropriateness, quality and consistency of official controls, as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The findings of the audit team in two establishments visited compared with the inspec- tions reports of the inspections/audits carried out by the regional milk specialists in two of the four regions visited (see chapter 5.6) indicate that the supervision by the central level (as foreseen in Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625) has not been sufficient to detect weaknesses in the control system.

The procedures and mechanisms in place ensure that controls are carried out uniformly and consistently, but do not guarantee that the controls are sufficiently thorough and in depth to detect shortcomings.

The supervision arrangements are not robust enough and have covered only narrow scopes and thus have not fully ensured the effectiveness, appropriateness, and quality of official controls, as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The audit team visited three dairy cow and one dairy sheep farm which had been in- spected by official veterinarians quite recently. The inspection reports reflected the ob- servations of the audit team related to three farms, where the conditions of milking hy- giene and use of VMPs and records kept were assessed as satisfactory. However, in one farm, milking hygiene was not complying with all requirements of Regulation (EC) No 7 852/2004. This was not recorded in the inspection report and consequently no corrective actions were requested. The CA ensured that an additional inspection would take place, and the necessary measures will be taken. Conclusions on controls over milk and colostrum production holdings

The official controls on compliance of dairy holdings with the legal requirements on an- imal health and welfare, identification and registration as well as the use of VMPs and milking hygiene are adequate and, with some exceptions, carried out correctly and well documented.

Some of the shortcomings noted by the DG(SANTE) audit team had not been identi- fied/recorded during previous inspections in relation to premises, hygiene, HACCP- based procedures, microbiological criteria, traceability and labelling (more details be- low). 5.6.3 General and specific hygiene requirements Legal requirements Article 4 of, and Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 3 of, and Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Findings

Major maintenance and general hygiene issues were noted by the audit team in one dairy establishment visited (producing ready-to-eat dairy products). The inspector had not recorded any non-compliances in the reports. The CCA accompanying the audit team in- formed on-spot that immediate actions are taken to suspend its activities.

Another dairy establishment visited was storing dairy products in a warehouse which had not been inspected by the milk specialist. The blueprint seen by the audit team did not indicate it was used for storing of milk products. 5.6.4 Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points based systems Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Findings

The audit team noted that the pest control programme in one establishment visited was insufficient. The inspection reports showed constant rodent activity but there was no root cause analysis to detect the reason (which was probably the access of rodents to milk powders in the storage containers for milk powder samples). 5.6.5 Microbiological criteria for foodstuffs Legal requirements Articles 3 and 4, and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

In one establishment visited, the audit team noticed that raw material packages (cheese in vacuum) in big carton boxes did not bear an identification mark and thus lacked relia- ble traceability. The operator stated, based on the accompanying documents, that these cheeses had been cut (sometimes also sliced or graded) and repacked in an approved es- tablishment. The later did not appear on the list of milk establishments, but on the list for packing establishments (see also paragraph 27) (2). The CA agreed to take measures regarding the non-compliant identification marking.

In one of the establishments visited, a dry store that had not been inspected by the re- gional milk specialist had approximately 50 tonnes of different types of milk and milk products powders without traceability or any other clear indication of their content as well as the purpose for use (for human consumption, feed or destruction). Some of the packages had passed their best before dates. In the same establishment, the audit team detected two milk powder packages in the main storage facility for which traceability could not be provided. The CA initiated investigations and measures immediately. Conclusions on official controls on FBOs' compliance with hygiene rules

The controls were not sufficiently in-depth in two of the four regions visited to detect all relevant shortcomings and/or, if detected, not recorded. In one establishment visited the enforcement measures available had not been applied although the plant had long- standing shortcomings and was not in compliance with EU requirements and its prod- ucts could pose a food safety risk. In another establishment, there were significant short- comings in relation to traceability and the categorisation of a large amount of products. These had not been covered by official controls and lacked the guarantees of being safe for human consumption.

recommendations.text: To ensure that sampling, especially shelf-life studies for ready-to-eat food able to support the growth of Listeria, are planned and applied by operators in line with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

citations.text: The audit team noted the following shortcoming in relation to requirements of Regula- tion (EC) No 2073/2005 on sampling and testing for Listeria monocytogenes (L. mono- cytogenes): a) Only one product (five subsamples) once in a year was send for detection of L. mon- ocytogenes while the operator produces a wide range of ready-to-eat products. This is not sufficient to ensure the safety of products; b) The operators had carried out shelf-life studies maintaining the samples at the low temperatures indicated for the storage on the packages (e.g.1 - 6°C) from their pro- duction until the end of shelf-life instead of taking into account of reasonably fore- seeable conditions of distribution, storage and use when determining the shelf-life of ready-to-eat products supporting the growth of L. monocytogenes; c) In some cases, analysis was carried out for compliance with 100 cfu of L. monocyto- genes, instead of absence in 25 g, although the FBO was not able to demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the CA, that the product will not exceed the limit of 100 cfu/g throughout the shelf-life; d) The samples in the studies seen comprised only testing a limited number of samples; e) An establishment, selling raw milk in retail packages, had established a shelf-life of six days and had sent only one subsample for Listeria analysis asking for numera- tion. The official had noted this non-compliance and had instructed to follow the rule for "not detected in 25 g". However, as only one sample had been sent for analysis the testing was still non-compliant as for a ready-to-eat products when five subsam- ples are required.

The audit team noted that environmental samples taken by the FBOs to detect the possi- ble presence of L. monocytogenes followed the Guidelines of the EU Reference Labora- tory on sampling as samples are taken during processing and included the drains as well, except in one case, where sampling takes place after cleaning. 5.6.6 Traceability, labelling and identification marking Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Article 5 of, and Chapter IV, Section IX, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 5 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings
